article_title: Examining the Academic Effects of Cross-age Tutoring: A Meta-analysis
citation: Chang, A., Mauer, E., Wanzek, J., Kim, S., Scammacca, N., & Swanson, E. (2025). Examining the academic effects of cross-age tutoring: A meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 37, 19. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09997-z
title: Vygotsky's social constructivist theory and the Zone of Proximal Development as the theoretical foundation for cross-age tutoring
description: The article grounds cross-age tutoring in Vygotsky's social constructivist theory, which posits that child development relies on "adult-supervised or peer-mediated experiences with social interaction, critical thinking, and problem solving." The Zone of Proximal Development represents "the range of tasks that a learner cannot yet perform independently, but could perform with the assistance of a more knowledgeable individual." In tutoring, the tutor serves as the more knowledgeable other, providing "support and scaffolding to help tutees accomplish tasks they cannot do alone." The article also draws on Chi's ICAP framework, noting that tutors engage in constructive learning by verbalizing explanations and may reach the interactive mode, "which represents the highest level of cognitive engagement."
requirements: A more knowledgeable tutor who can provide scaffolding within the tutee's zone of proximal development
constraints: The framework is theoretical; the article notes that empirical support comes from observed positive effects consistent with, not directly testing, the mechanism
target_learners: Older student tutors in grades 5 through 12
examples: The article interprets tutee gains as learning from a more knowledgeable other and tutor gains as practice of self-explanation, making implicit learning explicit
key_sources: Chang, A., Mauer, E., Wanzek, J., Kim, S., Scammacca, N., & Swanson, E. (2025). Examining the academic effects of cross-age tutoring: A meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 37, 19. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09997-z

article_title: The Strategies in Teaching isiXhosa Semantics in Foundation Phase: A Systematic Review
citation: Gobodwana, A., 2024, 'The strategies in teaching isiXhosa semantics in Foundation Phase: A systematic review', Reading & Writing 15(1), a493. https://doi.org/10.4102/rw.v15i1.493
title: Vygotskian mediation and behaviourist habit-formation framework for home-language learning
description: The article adopts two interchangeable theoretical frameworks as informants for home-language learning: Vygotsky's theory of child development centred on mediation, and Skinner's behaviourism. Vygotsky holds that mental processes are mediated by psychological tools such as language, acquired through interaction with the cultural environment; the article states "It should be easy for children to learn a second language, especially if their first language is well developed". Skinner views language learning as habit formation through reinforcement, with imitation of caregivers rewarded positively and divergence corrected by negative feedback.
requirements: Interaction with the cultural environment and interpersonal dialogue with adults or more experienced peers for tool acquisition
Reinforcement from the immediate surroundings for habit formation
constraints: The article notes a notable limitation of the mediation paradigm is Vygotsky's partial elucidation of the role of children's actions in the process of mediation
target_learners: Children from Grade R (aged 5–6 years) entering formal schooling
target_learning_goals: Second-language learning built on a developed first language
examples: The article uses the two frameworks to explain why children transition from their native language repertoire to a second language on exposure to speakers of other languages
key_sources: Gobodwana, A., 2024, 'The strategies in teaching isiXhosa semantics in Foundation Phase: A systematic review', Reading & Writing 15(1), a493. https://doi.org/10.4102/rw.v15i1.493

article_title: Effect of Teaching of Algebra through Social Constructivist Approach on 7th Graders' Learning Outcomes in Sindh (Pakistan)
citation: Bhutto Muhammad Ilyas, Khalid Jamil Rawat, Muhammad Tariq Bhatti, & Najeeb Malik. (2013). Effect of Teaching of Algebra through Social Constructivist Approach on 7th Graders' Learning Outcomes in Sindh (Pakistan). International Journal of Instruction, 6(1). http://www.e-iji.net
title: Vygotsky's social constructivist learning theory with three phases of learning
description: The article frames Vygotsky's social constructivism as the theoretical basis for its treatment: learning moves from the Zone of Approximate (actual) Development to the Zone of Proximal Development through "assistance or scaffolding provided by a mature or more experienced adult (or even peer)", and occurs only within a social and cultural setting, not in isolation. Johri's three phases — modeling or imitative learning, instructed learning (scaffolding), and collaborative learning — operationalize the theory, and the study applied all three to each algebra word problem.
requirements: Learning must take place within a cultural and social setting with adult or more-experienced peer assistance, per the article's account of Vygotsky
target_learners: grade-7 public school students learning algebra
target_learning_goals: converting word problems into algebraic equations and solving them
examples: The treatment teacher used loud thinking while solving problems (modeling), step-by-step two-way questioning with blackboard and charts (scaffolding), and six small groups each containing at least one bright student (collaboration)
key_sources: Bhutto Muhammad Ilyas, Khalid Jamil Rawat, Muhammad Tariq Bhatti, & Najeeb Malik. (2013). Effect of Teaching of Algebra through Social Constructivist Approach on 7th Graders' Learning Outcomes in Sindh (Pakistan). International Journal of Instruction, 6(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085370

article_title: Benefits and Meanings of Educating with Videogames in a Puerto Rican Sixth Grade Public School Classroom
citation: Vélez-Agosto, N. M. & Rivas-Vélez, A. (2018). Benefits and meanings of educating with videogames in a Puerto Rican sixth grade public school classroom. International Journal of Educational Technology, 5(1), 9-19. http://educationaltechnology.net/ijet/
title: Vygotsky's Socio-cultural Theory framing videogames as tools that reshape the learning environment and enable incidental learning
description: The study's theoretical framework is Vygotsky's Socio-cultural Theory, applied to human-computer interaction in classrooms. From this standpoint, "the insertion of videogames in the classroom is not simply the introduction of an extra learning tool, but a significant object that hopes to reshape the learning environment." Videogames are part of students' social and cultural context, clarify the motives of an activity through rules and parameters, and support incidental learning in which students acquire knowledge because it is the only way to continue playing. Extrinsic motivators like videogames are said to facilitate narrowing the gap described by the Zone of Proximal Development.
requirements: Videogames must be treated as significant objects integrated into the social and cultural context of students, not merely extra tools
constraints: The framework is applied specifically to English-as-a-second-language learning in a Puerto Rican public school context in this study
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary learning through incidental, ludic engagement
examples: Students approached videogames as entertainment and fostered competition without associating it with an educational task, which the authors read as incidental learning
key_sources: Vélez-Agosto, N. M. & Rivas-Vélez, A. (2018). Benefits and meanings of educating with videogames in a Puerto Rican sixth grade public school classroom. International Journal of Educational Technology, 5(1), 9-19. http://educationaltechnology.net/ijet/

article_title: Evaluating the Effects of Mother Tongue on Math and Science Instruction
citation: Behrmann, T. (2018). Evaluating the effects of mother tongue on math and science instruction. I. Sahin & T. Shelley (Eds.). Monument, CO, USA: ISTES Organization. https://www.istes.org
title: Vygotsky's sociocultural theory of language as a tool of social interaction frames the language-of-instruction problem
description: The monograph uses Vygotsky's Social Cultural Theory to explain why instruction in a language students do not use socially impedes learning. It states that acquiring language skills has a lot to do with social interactions, and that if a teacher cannot explain a difficult concept in the language the student understands well, the student must assimilate new concepts while also learning the language carrying them. The study relates to this theory by aiming to postulate differences in student interaction and communication of needs when French versus Kreyol is used.
requirements: Instruction and student social interaction must occur in a language the learner commands for the theory's predicted benefit to materialize
constraints: Applied in the monograph to the Haitian context where students' only contact with French is the classroom
target_learners: Haitian secondary students, mostly monolingual Kreyol speakers
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of math and science concepts through the medium of instruction
examples: The author designed the Kreyol-versus-French intervention so students could note the difference in their experience with each language in facilitating concept acquisition
key_sources: Behrmann, T. (2018). Evaluating the effects of mother tongue on math and science instruction. I. Sahin & T. Shelley (Eds.). Monument, CO, USA: ISTES Organization. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED623098

article_title: Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Learning in a Collaborative Context: A Case Study in Taiwan
citation: Tsai Pi-hua. (2015). Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Learning in a Collaborative Context: A Case Study in Taiwan. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 14(4). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Vygotskian sociocultural framework of mediation for pronunciation learning
description: The article frames pronunciation learning through Vygotsky's sociocultural theory, in which development moves from the inter-psychological (social) plane to the intra-psychological (individual) plane. It states that "knowledge is constructed through a process of collaboration, interaction, and communication among learners in social settings". The study uses this framework to interpret CAPT software, peers, and MP3 files as different kinds of mediation shaping learners' processes, and to interpret peer dialogue as mediating error awareness and self-regulation.
requirements: Learning must involve mediation by tools or peers through which knowledge is co-constructed in social settings
constraints: The article applies the framework interpretively to one case study; peer dialogue was not recorded, which the author notes limited the evidence
examples: The Collaborative CAPT Group's logs showed peers helping each other detect errors, brainstorm strategies, and revise production, which the author reads as validating the social nature of learning
key_sources: Tsai Pi-hua. (2015). Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Learning in a Collaborative Context: A Case Study in Taiwan. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 14(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1077659

article_title: The Impact of Computer and Mathematics Software Usage on Performance of School Leavers in the Western Cape Province of South Africa: A Comparative Analysis
citation: Garth Spencer Smith and Joanne Hardman. (2014). The impact of computer and mathematics software usage on performance of school leavers in the Western Cape Province of South Africa: A comparative analysis. International Journal of Education and Development using Information and Communication Technology, Vol. 10, Issue 1, pp. 22-40. http://ijedict.dec.uwi.edu/viewarticle.php?id=1678
title: Vygotskian mediation framework: computer software as a cultural tool mediating access to mathematics
description: The study draws conceptually on Vygotsky's (1978) theory that tools impact cognitive development. A fundamental premise is that basic biological processes "are transformed into higher cognitive functions through the use of culturally meaningful tools (such as language or, indeed a computer) during social interaction". Higher cognitive functions have social origins, first appearing as interpsychological functions and later turning inward as intrapsychological functions. Computer software, in this framing, can be seen to mediate a student's access to mathematics, which is the hypothesis informing the research.
requirements: The nature and the quality of mediation are crucial in the development of higher cognitive functioning and, relatedly, self-regulation.
target_learners: Senior Certificate (Grade 12) mathematics students in South African high schools
target_learning_goals: Mathematics attainment in the Senior Certificate examination
key_sources: Garth Spencer Smith and Joanne Hardman. (2014). The impact of computer and mathematics software usage on performance of school leavers in the Western Cape Province of South Africa: A comparative analysis. article_title: Improving dental student confidence through the use of simulated patient cases.
citation: Marsden JE, Deboo SP, Cripps M, Longridge NN, Aspden M, Fox K. (2025). Improving dental student confidence through the use of simulated patient cases. European Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.12867
title: Constructivist scaffolded simulation based on an interpretation of Vygotsky's theory and the Zone of Proximal Development
description: The authors designed the simulated patient cases using "a constructivist approach with scaffolded learning based on an interpretation of Vygotsky's Experimental Theory" as described by Higgins et al., set in a socio-cultural context. The premise is that "if learners are immersed in an environment where they experience others undertaking skills at a higher level than themselves, they would enter the 'Zone of Proximal Development' and develop the cognition to master such skills themselves". This is supported by reflective practice on concrete experiences, goal-setting to develop self-regulation, and consistent coaching-style feedback, drawing also on Bandura's account of mastery experiences as the foremost method of forming self-efficacy.
requirements: Educator support offered through each phase of planning, action and reflection; consistent and timely coaching-style feedback to facilitate effective self-reflection
constraints: The framework was applied to senior undergraduate dental students during a period without direct patient contact (COVID-19), as a transitional step between pre-clinical and clinical environments
target_learning_goals: Developing clinical competence and confidence through scaffolded simulation
Self-regulation through reflective practice and goal-setting
examples: The five simulated patient cases embedded pre-clinical, clinical and post-clinical activities with self-reflection and developmental goal-setting featured throughout
key_sources: Marsden JE, Deboo SP, Cripps M, Longridge NN, Aspden M, Fox K. (2025). Improving dental student confidence through the use of simulated patient cases. European Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.12867

article_title: Promoting medical competencies through international exchange programs: benefits on communication and effective doctor-patient relationships.
citation: Jacobs Fabian, Stegmann Karsten, Siebeck Matthias. (2014). Promoting medical competencies through international exchange programs: benefits on communication and effective doctor-patient relationships. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-14-43
title: Vygotsky's sociocultural learning theory as an explanatory framework for international exchange programs
description: The article applies Vygotsky's sociocultural approach, whose "central construct ... is the zone of proximal development (ZPD)", to explain how exchange programs produce learning. Learning is driven by social interaction between learners of different competence levels; extended by Damon's peer-conflict account, in which contradictions between the learner's beliefs and a more capable peer's explanations trigger reflection and new learning. The authors use this framework to predict that exchange programs affect not only soft skills but also job-specific medical competencies.
requirements: Interaction partners must differ in competence or culture so that a mental conflict arises between the learner's beliefs and the peer's explanations
constraints: The authors note the results "may only be applicable to the German health system; in other cultures, different competencies may be more important"
target_learners: clinical-stage undergraduate medical students in international exchange programs
target_learning_goals: job-specific medical competencies such as doctor-patient relationships and communication in a medical context
examples: The JU-LMU Link exchange placed German students in a community-based training program and clinical rotation in Jimma, Ethiopia, for six to twelve weeks
key_sources: Jacobs Fabian, Stegmann Karsten, Siebeck Matthias. (2014). Promoting medical competencies through international exchange programs: benefits on communication and effective doctor-patient relationships. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-14-43
